A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WARM research, with matching core methods and benchmark experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v2 ends with references; v3 includes readable supplementary Sections A–C.

before.justification: v2 reports original S3DIS and ScanNet segmentation results, component ablations, attention analyses, and optimization and token-sensitivity experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds loss, capacity, efficiency, numerical-stability, and integration experiments, including supplementary results.

M1.justification: The whitening–attention–coloring architecture, losses, and nearest-prototype prediction remain. v3 specifies adaptive eigenvalue regularization and rank-deficient inversion in Section 5.3 and Appendix B, refining v2's plain inverse formulation. It also introduces variants replacing FPS within existing segmentation frameworks. These are localized refinements and adaptations; the PDFs do not establish that retained benchmark experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate indoor few-shot point-cloud semantic segmentation on S3DIS and ScanNet with the same overall way/shot coverage. Added sampling protocols, point-count partitions, and model integrations operate within this retained dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 3–4 add MM-FSS while retaining AttMPTI, QGE, QGPA, COSeg, and FPS + min-dist. New integration comparisons evaluate COSeg and MM-FSS with WARM, and Appendix Table A3 compares VIP-Seg against VIP-Seg + WARM. These expand particular comparison sets without replacing the original baseline suite.

E3.justification: The main benchmark splits, training budgets, and mIoU evaluation remain, but v3 substantially expands the evaluation design. Additions include foreground-oversampling integration tests, controlled capacity and loss configurations, point-count/feature-dimension efficiency sweeps, and whitening tests partitioned by L > D versus L <= D. Diagnostics also gain mean-distance and anisotropy metrics. Newly stated block-eligibility criteria are additional documentation, not evidence of changed preprocessing.

E4.justification: v3 adds loss ablations, parameter-capacity controls, framework-integration tests, efficiency scaling, and eigenvalue-threshold sensitivity studies. It expands normalization diagnostics and token-count analysis across retained settings. The earlier optimization analysis survives in Appendix C.3/Figure A1; Figure 3 instead removes the support-prediction case-study panels.

E5.justification: v2's Table 1 caption specifies 1,000 FPS initializations per episode and aggregation across episodes by performance rank. v3 retains the original summary statistics but omits that repetition count and aggregation explanation, referring only to random seeds. This reduces statistical reporting detail without establishing any change in actual run counts.

E6.justification: The retained benchmark scores are unchanged, including WARM's overall 55.66 on S3DIS and 41.21 on ScanNet. However, v3 adds substantial comparator, loss, capacity, efficiency, regularization, and integration results. Table 2 also revises existing distance values from 284.18/288.81 to 282.61/271.18 and adds mean-distance and anisotropy measurements. These are expanded and revised findings, not improved retained benchmark scores.

T1.justification: v3 introduces formal mean-distance and instance-wise anisotropy definitions, spectral regularization rules, and treatment of rank-deficient inversion. Appendices A–B add supporting SVD and covariance derivations. These are limited mathematical additions; the compacted attention and loss equations otherwise preserve the earlier mathematics.

C1.justification: v2 claims state-of-the-art performance across FS-PCS benchmarks. v3 narrows this to S3DIS and describes ScanNet performance as competitive, with the results discussion distinguishing unimodal and multimodal comparisons. The central contribution—improving attention-based prototype construction through alignment and restoration—remains.

C2.justification: v3 expands the misalignment explanation from feature scale to mean displacement and anisotropy. It adds substantive discussion of singular covariance, noise amplification, information loss from excessive regularization, dataset-dependent token requirements, and runtime–memory tradeoffs. It also qualifies comparisons with multimodal methods by distinguishing prototype construction from richer pretrained features.

D1.justification: v3 adds a stated public code link, foreground block-eligibility thresholds, eigenvalue regularization and pseudoinverse details, and an SVD implementation intended to avoid precision loss. Parameter counts and resource measurements further document implementation costs. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although v2's explicit statement that the backbone remains frozen is omitted; that omission does not establish changed training.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted references to MM-FSS, VIP-Seg, language-driven semantic segmentation, and covariance-spectrum bounds. Its positioning more explicitly separates multimodal feature improvements from WARM's prototype-generation contribution and distinguishes sampling protocols. The broader positioning against heuristic FPS remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, motivation, method exposition, and results discussion undergo extensive rewriting and condensation. Experimental settings and results are reorganized, and the optimization discussion moves into the supplementary structure. These narrative changes extend beyond merely inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: The two-column document becomes a single-column layout with extensively resized and rearranged displays. Figure 3 transposes the examples and removes support-prediction panels; the token-sensitivity plot is redrawn and expanded. Several new tables are added, while the original training-stability Figure 5 is retained as supplementary Figure A1.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central argument: stronger comparator coverage leads to appropriately narrower performance claims, loss and capacity controls better isolate WARM's contribution, and numerical-stability experiments and implementation details address previously unexplained whitening behavior. These gains improve evidential support and reproducibility despite unchanged benchmark scores. They outweigh the limited reporting losses, particularly the omitted FPS repetition/aggregation explanation and explicit backbone-freezing statement.
